title: A Few Constrain Many: Correlation-Enhanced Learning of Many-Body Quantum Systems
abstract: Discovering properties of many-body quantum systems is challenging because of the large number of parameters to determine. Here, we show that correlations among quantum observables help reduce the complexity of quantum learning. A polynomial number of selected measurements can bound the values of exponentially many dependent yet unmeasured quantities, enabling efficient estimation of general functions of quantum states. We leverage this result to design correlation-informed learning algorithms that estimate key quantum resources, such as entanglement and magic, in systems of 100 qubits. They achieve a lower relative error than shadow tomography and neural-state methods by using information about a polynomial number of measured Pauli strings. These protocols are readily testable with today's quantum computers, as they do not require premeasurement entangling gates. Quantum constraints themselves are therefore a resource for exploring large quantum systems.
summary: This paper introduces correlation-enhanced learning algorithms to overcome the exponential scaling challenge in characterizing large quantum systems. By exploiting the mathematical constraints imposed by correlations between measured Pauli observables, the authors develop adaptive measurement strategies. These methods significantly improve the accuracy of estimating key quantum resources like entanglement and purity compared to standard tomography techniques.
main_problem: Characterizing the properties of large many-body quantum systems is computationally intractable due to the exponential number of parameters required for full state tomography.
main_result: By leveraging the correlations among a polynomial number of measured Pauli observables, the estimation of exponentially many unmeasured quantum quantities can be achieved with significantly lower relative error than existing methods.
method: The authors propose correlation-informed (CorInf) learning algorithms that adaptively select measurements based on theoretical bounds derived from Pauli operator commutation and anti-commutation relations.
model_or_system: The work is general for many-body quantum systems, demonstrated on systems up to 100 qubits, and specifically tested on 2D cluster states and rotated families of states.
key_observables: Entanglement, local purity, stabilizer Rényi-2 entropy, and expectation values of Pauli observables ($\mu_P$).
important_parameters: The measurement budget (number of Pauli strings measured) and the relative error achieved compared to standard methods.
main_assumptions: The protocols assume the measurement of Pauli observables and rely on deriving rigorous algebraic bounds from correlation information.
figures_summary: Figures compare the relative error of local purity and stabilizer Rényi entropy estimation using CorInf versus standard Classical Shadows (CS) and Neural-State methods (AGHDO), showing significant performance improvements for CorInf.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing theoretical bounds on information propagation using Pauli correlations (Appendix A/B) to developing adaptive measurement protocols (Appendix C) and finally demonstrating superior performance in estimating key quantum resources (Purity/Entropy) compared to non-adaptive methods.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, resource-efficient framework for quantum state tomography and resource estimation that is directly applicable to NISQ devices by minimizing the required number of entangling gates.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Measuring a small number of Pauli observables (here depicted as the biggest vertices in a connected network)–in fact, even a single Pauli coefficient–carries information about an exponential number of unobserved Pauli strings (the rest of the network). The strength of such correlations is quantified by a set of inequalities. Extremal expectation values (±1) are more informative, as they yield tighter bounds to unmeasured quantities. An experimentally convenient choice is to directly measure a set of commuting Pauli observables, as they share a common eigenbasis, i.e., a single preparation circuit.
